 Follow One of the Greatest Men in Country Music, the Grand Ole Opry’s Longest-Serving Member; “Whisperin’ Bill Turns 89
 Clara Awuse Sun, November 1, 2026 at 11:47 AM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. One of the Greatest Men in Country Music, the Grand Ole Opry’s Longest-Serving Member; “Whisperin’ Bill Turns 89 Happy birthday, Bill Anderson!
 The country music legend known as "Whisperin' Bill," once ranked among the 100 greatest men of country music, turns 89 today, Nov. 1, and more than six decades into his career, he's still making history.
 Born James William Anderson III in Columbia, South Carolina, in 1937, Anderson grew up in Georgia and went on to become one of the most prolific songwriters country music has ever seen. His famous nickname comes from his soft, conversational singing style, which became his signature sound.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Anderson joined the Grand Ole Opry on July 15, 1961. This year, the Opry celebrated his 65th anniversary as a member, a milestone no other singer has ever reached, making him the longest-serving member in the show's history. Opry executive producer Dan Rogers marked the occasion by calling the Opry Anderson's home for 65 years.
 His career on the charts is just as remarkable. Since 1958, Anderson has charted more than 80 singles on Billboard's country chart, with seven reaching No. 1. Those include "Mama Sang a Song" (1962), "Still" (1963), "I Get the Fever" (1966), "For Loving You" with Jan Howard (1967), "My Life (Throw It Away If I Want To)" (1969), "World of Make Believe" (1974) and "Sometimes" with Mary Lou Turner (1976).
 As a songwriter, his reach went far beyond country music. His songs have been recorded by artists including Ray Price, Porter Wagoner, Connie Smith, Kitty Wells, Dean Martin, James Brown, Aretha Franklin and Elvis Costello.
 Dolly Parton once praised him as a major force in the industry, saying it would be impossible to measure his worth.
 Advertisement Advertisement Even at 89, Anderson shows no signs of slowing down. After a "freak accident" forced him to cancel an Opry performance in August 2025, he bounced back and has continued performing throughout 2026.
 For a man who has spent 65 years on country music's most famous stage, it's clear the Opry's longest-serving member is still writing his story.
